prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and international trade reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: I opened with B001 first and B027 second, but on reflection the maturity and breadth arguments favour B027. It answers a central question: who gains and who loses from technological change and import competition. It does so with a conceptual framework (skill demand, tasks, polarization) and transparent quasi-experimental evidence on local labour markets. The core papers run from roughly 2003 to 2016 and have been replicated, extended and challenged, so the findings have been tested. Their influence reaches labour, trade, macro and policy. For a macroeconomist, the link between micro evidence on reallocation and aggregate adjustment is a strength. Attribution is also more tractable than in several other candidates. Autor is central to both strands, Hanson to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz to the long-run demand-and-supply-of-skills literature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the entry may be two distinct achievements, the task and skill-demand strand and the China-shock strand, under one citation. The three-name cap then forces a contestable choice between Katz and Dorn. Some China-shock magnitudes and persistence estimates have been revisited. The task framework also overlaps with Acemoglu's work, which was recognised in 2024, and with the recent prizes on labour and technology themes.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B027 first because it pairs a task-based framework with quasi-experimental trade-shock evidence. She argues the work answers a large question with wide policy impact, and that excluding Dorn is a real but unavoidable attribution cost.
responses.response: I agree that the combination of framework and credible new evidence is what lifts B027 above purely empirical or purely theoretical candidates, and it moved me toward ranking it first. I am less comfortable calling the Dorn exclusion merely unavoidable. It is a substantive cost for the trade-shock half of the citation, and I would not present the three-name set as uniquely correct.

responses.point: Friberg credits the local labour-market effects of import competition most cleanly to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He notes that the task framework has wider authorship, including Katz, so a three-name set leaves out Katz.
responses.response: This is the best argument for an alternative laureate set. If the committee narrows the citation to the trade shock, Dorn should replace Katz. I keep Katz because I want the citation to cover the technology and skill-demand side as well, and Katz anchors that literature. That choice depends on the committee accepting a joint technology-and-trade citation, and I regard it as an open question rather than a settled one.

responses.point: Hassler ranks Kiyotaki-Moore (B006) first. He sees collateral amplification as a foundational mechanism, and he restricts the award to Kiyotaki and Moore because the financial-accelerator strand overlaps with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I agree the Kiyotaki-Moore two-person attribution is cleaner than B027's, and I ranked B006 fourth with the same overlap concern. The mechanism is foundational but mainly theoretical, with thinner direct identification. B027 offers broader, tested empirical content and wider reach across fields. I would keep B006 as a serious later candidate and do not see its 2022 overlap as disqualifying.

responses.point: Krusell proposes only Autor and Hanson for B027. He argues the core contributions can be separated, that Katz also appears under B028, and that Acemoglu's parallel task work complicates attribution.
responses.response: A two-person award would be tighter, and the Acemoglu overlap is a fair concern. But Katz's skill-premium and education-technology work is the older foundation of this literature and fits B027 better than B028. Dropping him would leave the technology half of the citation resting on Autor alone. I would revisit this if the committee decides the citation should be limited to the China shock.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats tasks and trade shocks as one achievement or as two, and whether the final trio should be Autor, Hanson and Katz or Autor, Dorn and Hanson.
How much the persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and the overlap with Acemoglu's recognised task work, should reduce the case.
Whether Mian and Sufi (B001) is mature enough, and distinct enough from the 2022 prize, to justify moving ahead of or alongside B027.
Whether B012 (Helpman and Melitz) would be a cleaner two-person option, given its twenty years of confirmation and the question of credit to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Peter Klenow (credited in B017, not in my preferred configuration), and I have worked with Philippe Aghion and Antonin Bergeaud. I am also a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and a co-author of John Hassler, both committee colleagues, and an IIES colleague of both. None of these ties involves the credited names in B027, B001 or B012, so no recusal need is apparent for my preferred configuration. This is disclosed but not adjudicated.
